analysis.one_liner: Restores overtime pay to millions of salaried workers by raising the salary cutoff and updating it every three years.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 106 House members, was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee in June 2019 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal law, salaried workers in executive, administrative, or professional jobs can be denied overtime pay, no matter how little they earn, if they fall under the exemption. This bill writes a minimum salary cutoff into law: workers below the 40th percentile of salaried earnings in the lowest-wage region — the cutoff the Labor Department set in its 2016 rule, roughly $47,500 a year — would qualify for overtime pay of time-and-a-half for hours over 40. The cutoff would rise automatically every three years, and the Labor Department could set it higher. It would also require the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish quarterly data on salaried workers' earnings.
analysis.who_benefits: Salaried workers earning below the new cutoff — many of them working long hours in retail, food service, insurance, and office jobs — would become eligible for overtime pay they currently can be denied. Workers just above the cutoff could also benefit if employers raise salaries to keep them exempt.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes the 2016 Labor Department overtime rule — a salary cutoff set at the 40th percentile of full-time salaried earnings in the lowest-wage census region — the statutory minimum for exempting workers from overtime pay [S2][S3].
The cutoff would be updated automatically every three years without a new rulemaking process, so it could not simply sit still for decades as the current dollar threshold has [S2][S3].

The Secretary of Labor could set the threshold higher than the 40th percentile through regular rulemaking, and workers below the threshold would be paid time-and-a-half for hours worked over 40 per week [S3].
The Bureau of Labor Statistics would have to publish quarterly data on salaried workers' weekly earnings by census region, making the basis for the threshold publicly visible [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who currently pay salaries just above the old cutoff would owe overtime pay to newly covered workers, or would need to raise salaries or cap hours. That cost would fall most directly on labor-intensive industries such as retail, fast food, and insurance that rely on long hours from modestly paid salaried managers.

drawbacks.text: Employers — especially small businesses and nonprofits with tight budgets — would face higher payroll costs, which they could meet by cutting hours, converting salaried posts to hourly ones, or raising prices [S3].

A single national threshold pegged to the lowest-wage census region means the same cutoff applies everywhere; workers in lower-cost regions would be brought into overtime coverage at higher rates than their local labor market, while the Secretary's ability to set a higher threshold adds regulatory uncertainty for employers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of salaried workers who work more than 40 hours a week for pay near the cutoff, the gain is direct and concrete: either overtime pay or shorter hours. The cost is real but conventional — it is the cost employers always bear for overtime coverage, and it existed under the 2016 rule before a court set it aside. The main design weakness is the dependence on a lowest-wage-region benchmark, which makes the national threshold relatively modest, but that also makes it less disruptive.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Education and Labor Committee from June 2019 until the Congress ended in January 2021, with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Takano introduced the bill on June 11, 2019, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S1][S5].
106 House members cosponsored the bill — 105 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].
The bill's only action after its referral was the referral itself; the action history shows no committee markup, no report, and no floor vote [S5].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the bill died when that Congress expired [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in industries that rely on long hours from modestly paid salaried managers — retail, food service, and insurance among them — were spared the overtime or salary costs the bill would have imposed. Nothing changed for the workers the bill was meant to help.

for.name: Rep. Mark Takano
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 45 original cosponsors

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Bobby Scott (D-VA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the entire 116th Congress

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Democratic — 105 of 231 House Democrats cosponsored, against one of 197 House Republicans — and the bill died without any vote being held.

industries.note: These industries rely heavily on salaried assistant and store managers working 50-60 hours a week at modest salaries; the bill would have made those hours subject to overtime pay or forced salary raises.
Salaried claims adjusters, coordinators, and similar employees near the old cutoff would have become eligible for overtime, raising labor costs in office sectors.

industries.industry: Employers of salaried workers generally (small businesses and nonprofits)
industries.note: Any employer paying salaries just above the old threshold would owe overtime, need raises, or restructure hours; the automatic three-year updates would compound that cost over time.
